The Clarion County Register and Recorder's Office records them. It is in Suite 24 of the courthouse at 421 Main Street, Clarion, PA 16214, and the phone is (814) 226-4000. One elected officer on a four-year term runs the whole office, which also handles wills, estates and Orphans' Court filings.

The Recorder of Deeds side files land documents, military discharges, notary bonds and commissions, and powers of attorney. Land records run back to 1840, and the office holds a small number of deeds from Venango and Armstrong counties dating to 1800, the two counties Clarion County was carved from.

Anyone can look through the records on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30. Staff can't give legal advice, so a seller with a title question should go to a lawyer or the closing agent. This office is the last stop in a sale: once the deed is signed at closing, it is recorded here, and the recording puts the buyer's name in the public record.

Before closing day, ask the Register and Recorder's Office for the current Recorder of Deeds fee schedule. The cost of a deed depends on its page count and the number of names indexed, so the title agent should confirm the total in advance.

How you pay matters as much as how much. The office stopped accepting credit and debit cards on June 1, 2025, so a closing package should arrive with a check for the recording fee and a check for the transfer tax. If the title company handles recording, ask which of its checks covers each charge.

  • Bring checks, because cards have been refused at this counter since June 1, 2025.
  • Count the pages and the names on the deed, since both can raise the recording fee.
  • Ask whether the office can take the package by mail and whether a return envelope is needed.
  • Keep the recording receipt. It shows the date the new owner entered the record.

The state tax is one percent of what the property is worth, collected at recording by the county recorder. Under state rules the grantor and the grantee are both held jointly and severally liable, so a missed payment can be pursued against either party.

Counties usually collect an additional local realty transfer tax at the same time. The recorder forwards the 1 percent state share to the Department of Revenue, and local governments may split their share between the school district and the municipality. Ask the recorder which local rate applies to the borough or township where the house stands.

Some transfers are exempt from the tax.

  • Certain transfers among family members.
  • Transfers to governmental units and between religious organizations.
  • Transfers to shareholders or partners, and to or from nonprofit industrial development agencies.
  • Deeds to burial sites and farms, and property passed by will or intestate succession.

If you claim an exemption, ask the recorder what paperwork the office wants with the deed.

Many records can be searched online around the clock through the Infocon County Access System, a subscription service the county points people to. Searching in person is free during public hours, and the office keeps land records from 1840 forward.

A search helps a seller in a few ways. It shows whether an older mortgage was ever satisfied of record, whether a prior deed in the chain was recorded, and what the legal description said when the current owner bought. An heir who inherited a Clarion County house can check how the previous owner took title. Birth and death certificates after 1906 aren't kept here. They're filed with the state's vital records office, and the county page links to VitalChek for ordering.

Military discharge papers and adoption records are the exceptions to public access, so an owner who needs a discharge on file should ask the office how to request it.

Clarion County covers 610 square miles in Northwestern Pennsylvania, with 601 of them land. The seat is the borough of Clarion, which had 3,931 residents in 2020. The county had 36,680 residents in July 2025, 1.5 percent fewer than after the 2020 count.

With 23 building permits in 2025 and home values centered at $155,700, most sales here involve an existing house rather than new construction. Cold winters mean a buyer will ask about the furnace, the roof and the chimney.

Once the clerk records the deed, the buyer's name is in the public record, and the recording date becomes the date the new owner entered it. Keep the receipt with your closing papers. If you later need to prove who held title, or show a lender or title agent how you acquired the house, you can look the deed up in person for free during public hours or search online by subscription.

If something looks wrong on the recorded page, the office can't offer legal advice, so bring the question to your attorney or closing agent. A search of the record is also a good way to check that your old mortgage was satisfied of record and that every deed in the chain was recorded, which a buyer's title agent will check as well.

A short list prevents a delay at the recorder's counter.

  • Phone (814) 226-4000 to confirm the current fee schedule and any recording requirements for the deed.
  • Make sure the deed names the municipality where the property sits, since the local transfer tax follows that location.
  • Prepare checks for the recording fee and for state and local transfer tax. The office stopped taking cards on June 1, 2025.
  • If a family exemption or another exemption applies, ask what form the office needs filed with the deed.
  • Decide who will deliver the package and who receives the recorded original.

A quick sale for an heir or an owner behind on payments follows the same recording steps. The deed is still signed, still recorded in Clarion, and the transfer tax is still figured on the sale price. Allow time for the title agent to collect both checks, and confirm the amounts with the recorder's office the day before the closing.

faqs.q: Where do I take a deed in Clarion County?
faqs.a: Go to the Register and Recorder's Office in the Clarion County Courthouse, Suite 24, 421 Main Street, Clarion, PA 16214. The phone number is (814) 226-4000, and the public may inspect records on weekdays between 8:30 and 4:30.

faqs.q: Will the Clarion County office take a debit card?
faqs.a: No. The office stopped accepting credit and debit card payments on June 1, 2025, so bring a check for the recording fee and for the transfer tax.

faqs.q: What does Pennsylvania charge when a house changes hands?
faqs.a: The state tax is one percent of what the property is worth, and buyer and seller are both liable. Counties usually collect a local tax of their own at recording, so the total is higher than 1 percent.

faqs.q: How old are the land records held in Clarion?
faqs.a: Land records run back to 1840, and the office also holds a few deeds from Venango and Armstrong counties dating to 1800. Many of the records can be searched online through a subscription service.

faqs.q: Does Clarion County require an attorney at the recorder's counter?
faqs.a: The office gives no legal advice, so a lawyer or the closing agent should prepare the deed and answer questions about exemptions. The office records the document once it meets requirements and the fees are paid.
